title: Beyond long COVID: post-acute infection syndromes across Africa, a systematic review
abstract: Post-acute infection syndromes (PAIS) have gained global attention through Long COVID, yet many pathogens most closely linked to PAIS are endemic to Africa, where evidence remains scarce; a gap with implications for health equity and global health security. We aimed to systematically review the prevalence, clinical presentation, and associated factors of PAIS following non-COVID infections in Africa, and to identify priorities for future research. We conducted a systematic review, searching Medline, Embase, and grey literature until 7 November 2025 for studies in Africa reporting symptoms four or more weeks after acute infection. Case reports, case series, conference abstracts, secondary research, comments, and correspondence were excluded. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data on study characteristics, symptom prevalence, clinical presentation, and associated factors. As substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies, results were summarised descriptively. The study was registered on the Open Science Framework. Of 1,368 records, 65 studies were included, 42 on Ebola virus disease and 19 on chikungunya, with moderate to low risk of bias. Prevalence of PAIS ranged from 17.5% to 98.6% after Ebola and 12.1% to 78.6% after chikungunya. Musculoskeletal pain, ocular complications, headache, and fatigue predominated after Ebola; arthralgia was the hallmark of post-chikungunya disease. Substantial symptom burden persisted years after acute infection. Female sex, older age, and greater acute disease severity were the factors most frequently reported to be associated with persistent sequelae. An exploratory, non-systematic supplementary search additionally identified sex-specific consequences among female survivors including menstrual irregularities and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Despite scarce, heterogeneous, and geographically concentrated evidence, the reported prevalence of persistent symptoms among survivors is high, although the absence of comparison groups in most studies complicates attribution to the infection itself. Health systems in Africa must adapt to provide long-term survivor care, embedding follow-up into existing chronic care platforms. As pathogens endemic to Africa carry pandemic potential and expand geographically, understanding their chronic consequences is both a matter of health equity and an urgent global health security priority.

title: Development of a One-Step RT-LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12b Assay for Rapid On-Site Detection of Dabie Bandavirus
abstract: Abstract Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), caused by Dabie bandavirus (DBV), has rapidly spread to multiple countries worldwide since its discovery in 2009, posing a serious threat to global public health security. SFTS is a tick-borne disease, and people living in mountainous and hilly areas are at increased risk of infection, which highlights the urgent need for rapid, accurate, and field-applicable diagnostic strategies for DBV. In this study, LAMP primers and CRISPR sgRNA were designed based on the conserved region of the DBV L segment. A one-pot, one-step molecular assay integrating reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification (RT-LAMP) with CRISPR/Cas12b technology was established after systematic optimization of key parameters. The assay operates under isothermal conditions at 60 °C, delivering results within 40 min. Analytical evaluation demonstrated a limit of detection of 25.6 RNA copies per reaction. No cross-reactivity was observed with Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Chikungunya virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, Dengue virus, and Zika virus. Clinical validation using 42 specimens showed complete concordance with gold-standard qRT-PCR, achieving 100% sensitivity (30/30) and 100% specificity (12/12). For point-of-care application, fluorescence visualization was incorporated into the CRISPR/Cas-based detection workflow, enabling straightforward result interpretation. This integrated RT-LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12b platform provides rapid and specific detection of DBV through a simplified workflow that does not require complex instrumentation, supporting its potential application in resource-limited environments.

title: Cholesterol-Dependent Membrane Fluidity in Sindbis Virus Governs Viral Particle Stability and Infectivity
abstract: Cholesterol is a key biomolecule that regulates lipid bilayer fluidity, and cholesterol-rich domains in host cells and virions are critical for virion entry and egress. Here, using Alphavirus Sindbis virus (SINV) as a model, we combine new experimental methods and single-particle biological characterization to revisit how envelope cholesterol affects particle stability and the biological consequences for infectivity. To this end, we generated two SINV populations with a 3-fold difference in envelope cholesterol levels (SINV LC and SINV HC ) to assess how cholesterol affects SINV stability and infectivity. Transmission electron microscopy and dynamic light scattering showed minimal differences in morphology and size, indicating that cholesterol minimally alters virion structure. Electrochemical measurements between SINV LC and SINV HC particles revealed similar Zeta Potentials (ζ-potential ~ -31 mV), which implies that the surface distribution of the E1-E2 glycoprotein heterotrimers within the envelope is cholesterol-independent. Titer measurements showed that SINV HC retains nearly an order of magnitude more infectious particles than SINV LC when pre-exposed to 30 minutes of thermal stress, corresponding to a 1.25-fold faster decay rate for the low-cholesterol virions, with SINV LC and SINV HC showing values of 0.34/min and 0.27/min, respectively. Single-particle fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy analysis using the fluidity-sensitive dye DI-8-ANEPPS revealed a statistically significant increase (≥ 0.2 ns; p < 0.0001) in photon arrival times in the SINV HC population, indicating that elevated cholesterol enhances membrane rigidity. Because virion size and ζ-potential remained unchanged while fluorescence lifetimes increased with cholesterol level, these findings indicate that membrane fluidity is the primary parameter governing viral stability and subsequent infectivity.

title: Global patterns of genetic diversity and evolution in chikungunya virus E2 glycoprotein
abstract: The E2 glycoprotein of chikungunya virus (CHIKV) mediates host-cell attachment and entry and contains key antigenic determinants targeted by host immune responses. Variation in E2 can influence host interaction, immune recognition, lineage diversification, and epidemic fitness, it represents a biologically relevant target for assessing evolutionary pressures and epidemic dynamics. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of E2 genetic diversity using a dataset of sequences collected across regions, hosts, and epidemic periods. Diversity indices, neutrality tests, and haplotypes network analysis were applied to characterize evolutionary pressures acting on E2 glycoprotein. To assess the influence of geography, host, and time on viral population structure, we performed spatial–temporal stratification and analysis to assess clustering patterns across lineages and regions using Fixation index test (Fst). Nucleotide diversity varied considerably across time, with the pre-expansion period (pre-2004) showing the highest diversity (Pi = 0.085), while more recent outbreak periods exhibited comparatively reduced diversity (Pi = 0.012). Neutrality tests revealed signatures of both purifying and positive selection across the three CKIKV E2 lineages (negatively statistically significant Tajima D, Fu and Li’s D, and Fu and Li’s F tests, p -values < 0.05) supported by codon‐based analyses showing pervasive purifying constraint across the E2 gene but recurrent diversifying signals at lineage‐specific sites, notably codon 146 in the West African lineage, codons 220, 245, 247, and 254 in the Asian lineage, and codons 54, 56, 102, 145, 163, 177, and 350 in the East/Central/South/African lineage. Population structure analyses using Fst indicated significant genetic differentiation between regional populations, reflecting restricted gene flow and localized evolutionary trajectories. Haplotype network analysis highlighted distinct clustering patterns shaped by geography and epidemic waves, reflecting the persistence of lineage-specific signatures across regions. At the same time, reduced connectivity among recent outbreak strains point to more discrete intercontinental movement events, likely driven by human-mediated vector dispersal or travel-associated introductions. Collectively, these findings underscore the spatiotemporal evolution of CHIKV E2 glycoprotein and its implications for viral adaptation and immune evasion.

Population structure analyses using Fst indicated significant genetic differentiation between regional populations, reflecting restricted gene flow and localized evolutionary trajectories. Haplotype network analysis highlighted distinct clustering patterns shaped by geography and epidemic waves, reflecting the persistence of lineage-specific signatures across regions. At the same time, reduced connectivity among recent outbreak strains point to more discrete intercontinental movement events, likely driven by human-mediated vector dispersal or travel-associated introductions. Collectively, these findings underscore the spatiotemporal evolution of CHIKV E2 glycoprotein and its implications for viral adaptation and immune evasion.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在探讨基孔肯雅病毒(CHIKV)中E2糖蛋白的遗传多样性及进化,重点关注其在宿主细胞附着、免疫识别和谱系分化中的作用。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究分析了不同地区、宿主以及流行病时期的CHIKV序列数据集,以表征E2糖蛋白上的进化压力。
analysis_zh.methods: 研究人员使用多样性指数、中性检验和单倍型网络分析来评估遗传变异和进化动态,并进行了时空分层分析和固定指数(Fst)分析以评估种群结构。
analysis_zh.main_results: 核苷酸多样性在扩张前时期(Pi = 0.085)最高,而在近期的暴发时期则显著降低(Pi = 0.012)。中性检验显示在谱系中存在纯化选择和正向选择的信号,并确定了特定密码子作为分化信号的位点。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些发现突出了CHIKV E2糖蛋白的时空进化特性,揭示了可能影响免疫逃逸和病毒适应性的谱系特异性适应。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果为了解CHIKV的遗传进化提供了见解,有助于制定监测策略、疫苗开发以及理解病毒在暴发期间的适应过程。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的局限性在于其依赖于序列数据,可能无法全面捕捉所有进化压力。证据强度中等,因为它是基于遗传变异的计算和统计分析。

media_mentions.content: Clinical Hub News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More EN RegisterLog In AI Mode Medscape News UK Chikungunya Vaccine Withdrawn in UK After Safety Review Dr Sheena Meredith October 21, 2026 0 Add to Email Alerts Jump to Key Points The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has withdrawn the UK marketing authorisation for the IXCHIQ chikungunya vaccine. The move follows a safety review and advice from the Commission on Human Medicines. In a drug safety update, the MHRA said that the benefit-risk balance for the IXCHIQ chikungunya vaccine was “no longer considered favourable” and that the product was being removed from the UK market. Healthcare professionals should no longer prescribe, supply, or administer the IXCHIQ vaccine, and should dispose of any remaining stock in accordance with local policies. Any materials, systems, or communications referring to available UK vaccination options should be updated to remove the IXCHIQ vaccine. The MHRA said serious adverse reactions had occurred predominantly in older adults and patients with underlying medical conditions, but some were reported in individuals with no known health conditions, and some cases had resulted in hospitalisation or death. The withdrawal follows a previous drug safety update in February this year to restrict use of the vaccine. The MHRA said then that the vaccine was no longer indicated for adults over the age of 60, and was contraindicated in all individuals with hypertension, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and/or chronic kidney disease. Rare Fatal Reactions The February update followed global reports in 2025 of very rare fatal reactions and other serious adverse reactions, including viraemia and encephalitis. The vaccine was already contraindicated in people with immunodeficiency or immunosuppression as a result of disease or medical therapy, including IgA deficiency, a history of thymus disorder, or thymectomy. SUGGESTED FOR YOU Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne infection spread mainly by Aedes aegypti or Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, which bite during the day. It’s an alphavirus from the Togaviridae family and is found in subtropical regions of the Americas, Africa, Southeast Asia, India, and the Pacific region. Symptoms range from mild or nonexistent to severe, the latter causing fever with crippling joint pain lasting days or weeks. Other common symptoms include muscle pain, headache, nausea, fatigue, and rash. The disease may be misdiagnosed as dengue fever. Most patients make a full recovery, but arthralgia may sometimes persist for months or even years. Occasional cases of eye, neurologic, and heart complications have been reported, as well as gastrointestinal complaints. In older people the disease can contribute to death. There is no specific antiviral treatment for chikungunya. Supportive nursing care and relief of symptoms are the standard treatment. Live Virus Strain The IXCHIQ live attenuated chikungunya vaccine was approved in the UK in February 2025 and launched in mid-2025. It contained a live, weakened strain of the chikungunya virus, hence the need for strict adherence to contraindications and precautions to reduce the risk for serious side effects in people with weakened immune systems. Other Preventive Measures Healthcare professionals should advise individuals travelling from the UK to regions with known chikungunya transmission to consider other preventive measures, such as vaccination with an alternative vaccine, avoidance of mosquito bites through the use of netting or repellent, and adherence to health-related travel advice. The MHRA said patients who have previously received the IXCHIQ vaccine are at no risk if they did not experience side effects, and they do not need to take any specific action as a result of the latest regulatory decision. However, they should seek medical advice if they have experienced a suspected adverse reaction following IXCHIQ vaccination. Any such reactions should be reported via the Yellow Card scheme. Dr Sheena Meredith is an established medical writer, editor, and consultant in healthcare communications, with extensive experience writing for medical professionals and the general public. She is qualified in medicine and in law and medical ethics. News Chikungunya vaccine withdrawn after safety review The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency has advised healthcare professionals to stop prescribing, supplying or administering the IXCHIQ vaccine, as its benefit–risk balance is "no longer considered favourable”. Some recipients of the IXCHIQ vaccine, predominately older adults and individuals with underlying medical conditions, have reported serious adverse reactions, such as chikungunya-like symptoms and rare neurological events Yuri Arcurs/ Alamy Stock Photo The UK marketing authorisation for the IXCHIQ chikungunya live attenuated vaccine has been withdrawn after some recipients suffered serious side effects, leading to hospitalisation or death. The IXCHIQ vaccine (Valneva) was licensed by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) in February 2025 for use with adults, except those who are immunosuppressed. In a drug safety update published on 20 October 2026, the MHRA said that following the licensing of the vaccine, serious adverse reactions have been reported, including chikungunya-like symptoms and rare neurological events, such as encephalitis, with some cases resulting in hospitalisation or death. “These cases have occurred predominantly in older adults and individuals with underlying medical conditions but were also reported in individuals with no known health conditions,” it added. In February 2026, following the completion of a safety review and recommendations of the Commission on Human Medicines (CHM), the IXCHIQ vaccine was contraindicated for adults over the age of 60 years, as well as people with hypertension, cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus and/or chronic kidney disease. On 20 October 2026, following advice from the CHM, the MHRA published guidance, which instructed healthcare professionals to stop prescribing, supplying or administering the IXCHIQ vaccine, after it “concluded that the benefit-risk balance for the IXCHIQ chikungunya vaccine is no longer considered favourable”. Instead, health professionals should advise travellers of alternative measures to prevent chikungunya infection, including other available vaccines and avoiding mosquito bites, the guidance noted. An inactivated chikungunya vaccine is licensed for use in the UK, which contains adsorbed, recombinant chikungunya virus-like particles to protect against chikungunya infection. Derek Evans, travel medicine specialist and adjunct clinical professor at KGI School of Pharmacy in Los Angeles, told The Pharmaceutical Journal on 22 October 2026 that bite-avoidance measures should be considered the primary defence against chikungunya. In particular, he noted that the Aedes mosquito that spreads the virus has been found as far north as Italy and Spain, is active during the daytime and breeds around stagnant water. Travellers should wear long clothing where possible, use insect repellent, and change stagnant water, such as in a child’s toy, paddling pool, dog bowl or vase of flowers, frequently, Evans said. He continued that vaccination with the inactivated vaccine should be considered for travellers deemed to be at risk of chikungunya following a risk assessment. The MHRA drug safety update added: “There is no risk to individuals who have previously received IXCHIQ vaccination and did not experience side effects, and no revaccination or other medical intervention is required. Any individuals who have previously received IXCHIQ vaccination and experienced side effects are advised to seek medical advice and report to the Yellow Card scheme.” Graham Thoms, chief executive of Pharmadoctor, which supports more than 2,000 pharmacists, pharmacy technicians and nurses to deliver travel health and other services, told The Pharmaceutical Journal that the company had removed the IXCHIQ vaccine from its travel clinic service package. He said pharmacies could continue to use the Vimkunya vaccine (Bavarian Nordic), adding that this was already the more widely used chikungunya vaccine among partner pharmacies because it could be given to a wider age range of patients. full_text: BACKGROUND Aedes vittatus, an emerging invasive species and arboviral vector with high ecological plasticity and dispersal capacity, is expanding in the Caribbean, being detected in the Dominican Republic, Cuba, and Jamaica and recently in Yucatán, Mexico.OBJECTIVESThis study aimed to provide evidence of the establishment of Ae. vittatus in Haiti.METHODSLarval surveys were conducted in 18 localities within 12 municipalities in the North and Northeast departments of Haiti. Specimens were identified morphologically and confirmed by COI-based DNA barcoding.FINDINGSWe report, for the first time, the detection of the invasive vector Ae. (Fredwardsius) vittatus in Haiti, confirmed morphologically and molecularly, with the species detected in half of the municipalities sampled. Phylogenetic analyses placed Haitian specimens within a Caribbean/American group, closely related to sequences from Mexico. Additional mosquito species were identified, including first records of Culex garciai and Culex interrogator in Haiti.MAIN CONCLUSIONSGiven its potential role as a vector of chikungunya, dengue, Zika and yellow fever, continued entomological surveillance and early detection in the Caribbean and the Americas are needed. MATERIALS AND METHODS Study area - The survey was conducted in the North and Northeast departments of Haiti, restricted to the extensive, low-elevation coastal zones of both regions. Following the 2010 earthquake that struck the Port-au-Prince area, the North department experienced the arrival of more than 2.3 million people, resulting in rapid and largely unplanned urban expansion, increasing the suitable area for urban mosquitoes.( 6 ) This department is therefore densely populated (500 inhabitants/km2), in contrast to the Northeast, where population density is approximately 240 inhabitants/km2. The climate varies from tropical monsoon (North Department) to tropical savanna (Northeast Department), with mean annual temperatures of 24 to 28oC and seasonal rainfall (April to November), averaging between 1,000 and 1,500 mm per year, with a decreasing gradient from the coast toward the interior.The study area, located mainly within the coastal plains surrounding the departmental capital, Cap-Haïtien, extends from Limbé (19o42’N, 72o24’W) in the west to Ouanaminthe (19o29’N, 71o46’W), located on the Dominican border, 75 km east of Limbé, following the coastal fringe and reaching up to 20 km inland. It is characterised by moderately low relief, with most of the coastline and its surroundings lying at elevations generally below 100 m in urban and peri-urban zones. Mosquito sampling - Between October 7 and October 31, 2025, during the latter part of the rainy season, surveys were conducted in urban, peri-urban and rural areas across both departments. A total of 23 larval habitats were collected in 18 localities within 12 communes (seven in the North and five in the Northeast) (Fig. 1). Sampling time did not exceed 3 h per commune. Mosquito larvae were collected from peridomestic and public spaces. For each sample site, some collected larvae were mounted on slides, while others were reared to the adult stage, and both types of specimens were deposited in the ARIM-IRD collection.( 7 ) Geographical coordinates and data were uploaded to the GBIF platform.Fig. 1:location of the sampling sites. (A) Situation map of Haiti within Caribbean countries with presence (green area) and location of capture points (red dots) of Aedes vittatus in neighbouring countries; (B) Delimitation of study area in Haiti (blue rectangle) and location capture (red dots) of Ae. vittatus in Haiti and the Dominican Republic; (C) Location of the breeding site of Ae. vittatus in the study area (red dots) and other collection sites negative to Ae. vittatus (grey dots) (Table). Ethics statement - This study was conducted with authorisation from the Haitian Ministry of Environment, and the importation of mosquitoes from Haiti to France was approved by the Departmental Directorate for Population Protection (DDPP). Morphological and molecular identification - The invasive species Ae. vittatus was identified using European,( 8 ) African( 9 ) and Sahelian( 10 ) taxonomic keys, and confirmed with the species redescription of Huang.( 11 ) Five samples from the localities Quartier Morin (two adults: QUA003-Haiti06 and 07) and Lory, Milot (two adults: MIL001-Haiti08 and 09 and one larvae: MIL004LAV-10) were used for molecular identification. Mosquito DNA was extracted with the Qiagen Blood&tissue kit (Qiagen, Valencia, USA). Mosquitoes were individually homogenised with three metal beads in a Qiagen TissueLyserII at 30 Hz for 3 min. The remainder of the protocol followed the manufacturer’s instructions. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was performed in duplicate for each sample to validate the species identification through a universal invertebrate-specific primer pair LCO1490 (5′-GGT CAA CAA ATC ATA AAG ATA TTG G-3′) and HCO2198 (5′-TAA ACT TCA GGG TGA CCA AAA AAT CA-3′) to amplify a 658-bp fragment of the mitochondrial gene cytochrome c oxidase subunit I barcoding region (COI).( 12 ) PCR reactions were performed in a total volume of 35 μL, containing 17.5 μL Invitrogen TM PlatinumTM Hot Start PCR 2X Master Mix, 0.35 μL of each primer, 9.8 μL of biology grade water, and 7 μL of DNA. PCR amplification products were sent to Macrogen (Macrogen Europe, Amsterdam, the Netherlands) for Sanger sequencing. A Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) analysis was conducted in the National Centre for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) GenBank database to explore species identification based on the amplified and sequenced molecular product.( 13 ) Sequence assembly, alignment and phylogenetic analyses - Forward and reverse reads of four samples, as one of the five samples (MIL004LAV-10) did not amplify, were assembled and edited to generate consensus sequences using CodonCode Aligner v12.0.4 (https://www.codoncode.com/aligner). Sequence alignments were performed with MAFFT v7 via the online server (https://mafft.cbrc.jp/alignment/server/) using default parameters.( 14 ) The resulting alignments were visually inspected and manually edited in AliView v1.28.( 15 ) The best-fit nucleotide substitution model was determined using jModelTest2 through the CIPRES Science Gateway (https://www.phylo.org/) under default settings.( 16 ) Mitochondrial sequences, including COI marker sequences of Aedes spp., were retrieved from GenBank (accession numbers provided in the phylogenetic tree). The dataset comprised sequences from Africa, Asia, Europe, the Caribbean, and a recently generated sequence from Mexico.Phylogenetic relationships among Ae. vittatus sequences were inferred using BEAST v1.10.5, applying a General Time Reversible substitution model+r returned by jModelTest2, a strict molecular clock, and a coalescent constant size tree prior. Psorophora ferox was designated as the outgroup.( 17 ) Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analyses were run for 10 million generations, with trees sampled every 100 generations. Effective sample sizes (ESS) were assessed using Tracer v 1.7.2,( 18 ) with values > 200 considered adequate. Convergence and stationarity were assessed by examining parameter traces, and the first 25% of samples were discarded as burn-in prior to summarising posterior probabilities. The final phylogenetic tree was visualised and edited using FigTree v1.4.4.( 19 ) Network analysis - Analyses at the intraspecific level were performed on datasets that encompassed only Ae. vittatus sequences. The genetic differentiation between specimens belonging to the major phylogroups inferred by the phylogenetic analyses of the combined dataset was assessed for each COI gene using DnaSP v.6.12.03.( 20 ) Haplotype networks were constructed using the median-joining method,( 21 ) which has the ability to deal with missing data as well as to infer ancestral haplotypes. This method also performs well against or outperforms other network approaches.( 22 ) It was implemented using the software PopART v1.7,( 23 ) with epsilon value set to 0 in order to minimise alternative median networks. The resulting networks were visualised and edited in Inkscape v1.2.2 (https://inkscape.org/). RESULTSDuring the sampling period, Ae. vittatus was detected in eight of the 23 sites (34.7%) across six municipalities in northern Haiti: Cap-Haïtien, Quartier Morin, Milot, Limbé, Trou du Nord, and Terrier Rouge (Table). The species was found alone in three of these sites and co-occurred with Ae. albopictus (three sites) and Ae. aegypti (two sites). Breeding habitats included diverse peridomestic and public environments across urban, peri-urban, and rural settings, such as water storage containers, groundwater accumulations, poultry waterers, wastewater channels, puddles, and tree root cavities. These habitats were generally devoid of vegetation and varied in water volume and organic content. Eight additional mosquito species were recorded, including Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, Culex quinquefasciatus, Culex garciai, Culex interrogator, Culex nigripalpus, Psorophora confinnis and Psorophora pygmaea. SimonèteLimbéLIB00319.70906-72.40326Stagnant water on road14/10/2025 Psorophora pygmaea Morphological identification - Both larval stages and adults obtained from breeding were examined, and diagnostic characters for the principal life stages for Ae. vittatus are summarised as follows (Fig. 2).Fig. 2: Aedes vittatus: morphological characteristics of the larval stage. (A) Detail of abdominal segments VIII-X (the long anal papillae are missing); (B) head showing single setae 5-C and 6-C (arrows); (C) mentum; (D) comb VIII with eight spines; (E) detail of the pecten teeth with two or three denticles; (F) atypical pecten with the rare presence of two teeth (instead of one, arrows) inserted distal to the 1-S setae. Female - Head with a dark proboscis with a median scattering of pale yellowish scales. Thorax: scutum with acrostichal setae; three pairs of distinct, small, white spots of narrow scales on the anterior two-thirds of the scutum; scutellum with broad white scales on all three lobes; lower mesepimeral setae present. Legs: tibia with a median white ring, tarsomeres III-1-4 with large basal white bands, tarsomere III-5 entirely white. Abdomen: tergite I with a large median white spot. Male genitalia - Gonocoxite elongated, without basal and apical lobes. The gonostyle has a very characteristic shape, strongly enlarged and globose at its tip, with a long, strongly curved apical spine located at the base of the globose part. The claspette is large, with a narrow base, and distinctly swollen from its middle. Larva (Fig. 2) - Head: setae 5-C single or sometimes double, 6-C single. Abdomen: setae 6-I-IV usually with two long branches; pecten with 19-25 very closely spaced spines, with 3-4 basal denticles; only the most distal spine (rarely two) more widely spaced and implanted beyond seta 1-S; comb of eight (6-10) scales in a single irregular row; saddle incomplete without marginal spicules; 1-X single, 2-X with 5 branches; four precratal setae; anal papillae long, about four times as long as saddle, slender and tapered. Molecular identification - Morphological identification was confirmed with COI-based DNA barcoding. The Ae. vittatus specimens (Haiti_06, Haiti_07, Haiti_08, Haiti_09) clustered with Caribbean and American haplotypes (Cuba, Jamaica, the Dominican Republic, and Mexico).( 3 , 5 (24-27) In the haplotype network, they share closely related haplotypes separated by only a small number of mutations, suggesting a high level of genetic similarity within this group, particularly with Mexican populations( 5 ) (Fig. 3). This Caribbean/American cluster appeared distinct from African haplotypes and from most Asian haplotypes, which form separate groups within the network. The observed pattern is consistent with the Caribbean/American lineage being genetically distinct from African and most Asian haplotypes, although the limited number of specimens and the use of a single mitochondrial marker preclude firm conclusions about the geographic origin or pathways of introduction. The COI-based DNA barcoding confirmed the identification of Ps. pygmaea, Cx. quinquefasciatus, Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus and Cx. interrogator, with the latter showing high similarity to GenBank reference sequences (99.67% identity; MT999299.1). For Cx. garciai, no reference sequences are currently available in GenBank; therefore, we generated the first COI sequences for this species in this study. Sequences of Ae. vittatus were submitted to GenBank under accession numbers PZ344144, PZ344145, PZ344146 and PZ344147. Sequences of Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, Cx. garciai, Cx. interrogator, Cx. quinquefasciatus and Ps. pygmaea have been deposited under accession numbers PZ878903, PZ878904, PZ878905, PZ878906, PZ878907, PZ878908, PZ878909, PZ878910, PZ878911.Fig. 3:haplotype network and phylogenetic tree resulting from the analysis of the cytochrome c oxidase subunit I barcoding region (COI) dataset. The haplotype network reconstruction considers missing data and gap. Values between parentheses on nodes indicate the inferred number of mutation steps between haplotypes or ancestral haplotypes (symbolised by a black node). The phylogenetic tree corresponds to the results of a Bayesian inference analysis (see text for details). DISCUSSIONSpecies identification was confirmed morphologically and by COI-based DNA barcoding. Haitian Ae. vittatus specimens clustered with Caribbean and American haplotypes (Cuba, Jamaica, Dominican Republic, and Mexico) and were clearly distinct from African and most Asian lineages (Fig. 3). This pattern is consistent with a shared regional genetic background within the Caribbean/American group, although more molecular markers, more populations and specimens are needed to confirm this hypothesis. Detection of Ae. vittatus in one-third of the sampled habitats and half of the surveyed communes, despite limited sampling, indicates that the species is present at multiple localities in northern Haiti. However, given the limited sampling effort, further surveys are needed to assess its wider distribution and establish the extent of its establishment.Its absence from earlier surveys in 2013,( 6 ) combined with its detection in the Dominican Republic in 2019,( 3 ) is consistent with a relatively recent arrival on Hispaniola. However, the available data do not allow us to determine the timing or pathway of introduction. Passive transport via water holding containers and other goods may have contributed to its spread, but the relative importance of each introduction pathway remains unknown. Passive transport via water-holding goods is a well-documented pathway for mosquito invasions, and the species’ desiccation-resistant eggs further enhance its dispersal potential. Genetic similarity with recently detected Mexican populations( 5 ) suggests strong regional connectivity, although the direction of spread remains unclear. Additional sampling across Haiti and the use of nuclear and/or genomic markers will be necessary to clarify the distribution, population structure and introduction pathways of the species.Current socio-environmental conditions in Haiti, including population displacement, informal settlements, inadequate water infrastructure, and unmanaged waste, favour the proliferation of container-breeding mosquitoes and may provide favourable conditions for the establishment of Ae. vittatus. Sequence alignments were performed with MAFFT v7 via the online server (https://mafft.cbrc.jp/alignment/server/) using default parameters.( 14 ) The resulting alignments were visually inspected and manually edited in AliView v1.28.( 15 ) The best-fit nucleotide substitution model was determined using jModelTest2 through the CIPRES Science Gateway (https://www.phylo.org/) under default settings.( 16 ) Mitochondrial sequences, including COI marker sequences of Aedes spp., were retrieved from GenBank (accession numbers provided in the phylogenetic tree). The dataset comprised sequences from Africa, Asia, Europe, the Caribbean, and a recently generated sequence from Mexico.Phylogenetic relationships among Ae. vittatus sequences were inferred using BEAST v1.10.5, applying a General Time Reversible substitution model+r returned by jModelTest2, a strict molecular clock, and a coalescent constant size tree prior. Psorophora ferox was designated as the outgroup.( 17 ) Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analyses were run for 10 million generations, with trees sampled every 100 generations. Effective sample sizes (ESS) were assessed using Tracer v 1.7.2,( 18 ) with values > 200 considered adequate. Convergence and stationarity were assessed by examining parameter traces, and the first 25% of samples were discarded as burn-in prior to summarising posterior probabilities. The final phylogenetic tree was visualised and edited using FigTree v1.4.4.( 19 ) Network analysis - Analyses at the intraspecific level were performed on datasets that encompassed only Ae. vittatus sequences. The genetic differentiation between specimens belonging to the major phylogroups inferred by the phylogenetic analyses of the combined dataset was assessed for each COI gene using DnaSP v.6.12.03.( 20 ) Haplotype networks were constructed using the median-joining method,( 21 ) which has the ability to deal with missing data as well as to infer ancestral haplotypes. This method also performs well against or outperforms other network approaches.( 22 ) It was implemented using the software PopART v1.7,( 23 ) with epsilon value set to 0 in order to minimise alternative median networks. The resulting networks were visualised and edited in Inkscape v1.2.2 (https://inkscape.org/).

The species was found alone in three of these sites and co-occurred with Ae. albopictus (three sites) and Ae. aegypti (two sites). Breeding habitats included diverse peridomestic and public environments across urban, peri-urban, and rural settings, such as water storage containers, groundwater accumulations, poultry waterers, wastewater channels, puddles, and tree root cavities. These habitats were generally devoid of vegetation and varied in water volume and organic content. Eight additional mosquito species were recorded, including Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, Culex quinquefasciatus, Culex garciai, Culex interrogator, Culex nigripalpus, Psorophora confinnis and Psorophora pygmaea. diagnostic characters for the principal life stages for Ae. vittatus are summarised as follows (Fig. 2).Fig. 2: Aedes vittatus: morphological characteristics of the larval stage. (A) Detail of abdominal segments VIII-X (the long anal papillae are missing); (B) head showing single setae 5-C and 6-C (arrows); (C) mentum; (D) comb VIII with eight spines; (E) detail of the pecten teeth with two or three denticles; (F) atypical pecten with the rare presence of two teeth (instead of one, arrows) inserted distal to the 1-S setae. Female - Head with a dark proboscis with a median scattering of pale yellowish scales. Thorax: scutum with acrostichal setae; three pairs of distinct, small, white spots of narrow scales on the anterior two-thirds of the scutum; scutellum with broad white scales on all three lobes; lower mesepimeral setae present. Legs: tibia with a median white ring, tarsomeres III-1-4 with large basal white bands, tarsomere III-5 entirely white. Abdomen: tergite I with a large median white spot. Male genitalia - Gonocoxite elongated, without basal and apical lobes. The gonostyle has a very characteristic shape, strongly enlarged and globose at its tip, with a long, strongly curved apical spine located at the base of the globose part. The claspette is large, with a narrow base, and distinctly swollen from its middle. Larva (Fig. 2) - Head: setae 5-C single or sometimes double, 6-C single. Abdomen: setae 6-I-IV usually with two long branches; pecten with 19-25 very closely spaced spines, with 3-4 basal denticles; only the most distal spine (rarely two) more widely spaced and implanted beyond seta 1-S; comb of eight (6-10) scales in a single irregular row; saddle incomplete without marginal spicules; 1-X single, 2-X with 5 branches; four precratal setae; anal papillae long, about four times as long as saddle, slender and tapered. Molecular identification - Morphological identification was confirmed with COI-based DNA barcoding. The Ae. vittatus specimens (Haiti_06, Haiti_07, Haiti_08, Haiti_09) clustered with Caribbean and American haplotypes (Cuba, Jamaica, the Dominican Republic, and Mexico).( 3 , 5 (24-27) In the haplotype network, they share closely related haplotypes separated by only a small number of mutations, suggesting a high level of genetic similarity within this group, particularly with Mexican populations( 5 ) (Fig. 3). This Caribbean/American cluster appeared distinct from African haplotypes and from most Asian haplotypes, which form separate groups within the network. The observed pattern is consistent with the Caribbean/American lineage being genetically distinct from African and most Asian haplotypes, although the limited number of specimens and the use of a single mitochondrial marker preclude firm conclusions about the geographic origin or pathways of introduction. The COI-based DNA barcoding confirmed the identification of Ps. pygmaea, Cx. quinquefasciatus, Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus and Cx. interrogator, with the latter showing high similarity to GenBank reference sequences (99.67% identity; MT999299.1). The haplotype network reconstruction considers missing data and gap. Values between parentheses on nodes indicate the inferred number of mutation steps between haplotypes or ancestral haplotypes (symbolised by a black node). The phylogenetic tree corresponds to the results of a Bayesian inference analysis (see text for details).
full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONSpecies identification was confirmed morphologically and by COI-based DNA barcoding. Haitian Ae. vittatus specimens clustered with Caribbean and American haplotypes (Cuba, Jamaica, Dominican Republic, and Mexico) and were clearly distinct from African and most Asian lineages (Fig. 3). This pattern is consistent with a shared regional genetic background within the Caribbean/American group, although more molecular markers, more populations and specimens are needed to confirm this hypothesis. Detection of Ae. vittatus in one-third of the sampled habitats and half of the surveyed communes, despite limited sampling, indicates that the species is present at multiple localities in northern Haiti. However, given the limited sampling effort, further surveys are needed to assess its wider distribution and establish the extent of its establishment.Its absence from earlier surveys in 2013,( 6 ) combined with its detection in the Dominican Republic in 2019,( 3 ) is consistent with a relatively recent arrival on Hispaniola. However, the available data do not allow us to determine the timing or pathway of introduction. Passive transport via water holding containers and other goods may have contributed to its spread, but the relative importance of each introduction pathway remains unknown. Passive transport via water-holding goods is a well-documented pathway for mosquito invasions, and the species’ desiccation-resistant eggs further enhance its dispersal potential. Genetic similarity with recently detected Mexican populations( 5 ) suggests strong regional connectivity, although the direction of spread remains unclear. Additional sampling across Haiti and the use of nuclear and/or genomic markers will be necessary to clarify the distribution, population structure and introduction pathways of the species.Current socio-environmental conditions in Haiti, including population displacement, informal settlements, inadequate water infrastructure, and unmanaged waste, favour the proliferation of container-breeding mosquitoes and may provide favourable conditions for the establishment of Ae. vittatus. The species exhibits high ecological plasticity, colonising a wide range of artificial and natural habitats. Its tolerance to desiccation, salinity, and high temperatures further enhances its invasion potential.( 28 ) Co-occurrence with Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus raises questions about interspecific interactions and future ecological dynamics in urban environments. Notably, we also reported Cx. garciai and Cx. interrogator from Haiti for the first time. Morphological identification of Cx. interrogator was supported by molecular results, showing high sequence identity but lower query coverage, likely reflecting partial sequences or trimming.From a public health perspective, Ae. vittatus is competent for multiple arboviruses, including dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever.( 29 , 30 ) Its establishment adds complexity to Haiti’s epidemiologic context, which already includes endemic dengue, recurrent chikungunya outbreaks, and ongoing malaria and filariasis transmission. Notably, ecological niche models suggest that Ae. vittatus could find year-round suitable conditions across coastal regions of the Gulf of Mexico and extend into the southern Atlantic states of the United States, as well as large areas of Mexico and Central America.( 31 ) This potential geographic suitability highlights the possibility of further spread into North America, Central and South America and underscores the need for strengthened surveillance and preparedness beyond the Caribbean.Our findings provide the first confirmed record of Ae. vittatus in Haiti and demonstrate its presence in multiple locations. Further surveillance is needed to determine its distribution, extent of establishment, ecological interactions, and potential contribution to arbovirus transmission in the region and beyond.
full_text_sections.other: REVIEWER #1The abstract adequately summarizes the study and highlights the first detection of Aedes vittatus in Haiti. This finding fills an important geographical gap and has clear relevance for mosquito surveillance in the Caribbean and the Americas. The manuscript should avoid strong conclusions, as these interpretations are based on limited sampling and a single mitochondrial marker. Inconsistencies in dates and sites / localities should also be corrected. References are generally relevant and updated, but their formatting should be standardized. AUTHORS’ RESPONSE TO THE REVIEWERSDear Prof. Ricardo Lourenço-de-Oliveira and Maria Clara Carvalho:We are pleased to submit the letter of response to the referees for the manuscript entitled “Aedes vittatus in Haiti: continued expansion across the Caribbean and implications for the Americas” for consideration in Memórias do Instituto Oswaldo Cruz, on behalf of my co-authors. Here are our point-by-point responses. The comments are in bold and our responses are in regular text in blue. We have added the modifications to a track changes version of the manuscript in red.Reviewer comments:The abstract adequately summarizes the study and highlights the first detection of Aedes vittatus in Haiti. This finding fills an important geographical gap and has clear relevance for mosquito surveillance in the Caribbean and the Americas.We sincerely thank you for your positive and constructive and positive comments. We are pleased that you find the study relevant and that the detection of Aedes vittatus in Haiti fills an important geographical gap for mosquito surveillance in the Caribbean and the Americas.The manuscript should avoid strong conclusions, as these interpretations are based on limited sampling and a single mitochondrial marker.We agree and we have moderated the strength of our conclusions throughout the manuscript, particularly in the Abstract and Discussion, to better reflect the limitations of our study, including the relatively limited sampling effort and the use of a single mitochondrial marker (COI). We now explicitly acknowledge these limitations and clarify that our interpretations regarding establishment, regional expansion and spread should be considered with caution.In the abstract, we changed for: “We report, for the first time, the detection of the invasive vector Aedes (Fredwardsius) vittatus in Haiti, confirmed morphologically and molecularly, with the species detected in half of the municipalities sampled. Phylogenetic analyses placed Haitian specimens within a Caribbean/American group, closely related to sequences from Mexico.” (lines 31-34). Also in the main conclusion of the abstract: “Given its potential role as a vector of chikungunya, dengue, Zika and yellow fever, continued entomological surveillance and early detection in the Caribbean and the Americas are needed.” (lines 35-36).In the results, we substitute the sentence: “The results support a common Asian-rather than African or European origin with regional spread in the Caribbean.”, with “The observed pattern is consistent with the Caribbean/American lineage being genetically distinct from African and most Asian haplotypes, although the limited number of specimens and the use of a single mitochondrial marker preclude firm conclusions about the geographic origin or pathways of introduction.” (lines 172-176).In the conclusion, we substitute: “This pattern supports a shared regional origin and spread within the Caribbean rather than multiple independent introductions from the Old World.”, for “This pattern is consistent with a shared regional genetic background within the Caribbean/American group, although more molecular markers, more populations and specimens are needed to confirm this hypothesis.” (lines 182-184). Also, ”.. indicates that the species is present at multiple localities in northern Haiti. However, given the limited sampling effort, further surveys are needed to assess its wider distribution and establish the extent of its establishment.” (lines 185-188).Also, we changed “...is compatible with a relatively recent arrival on Hispaniola. However, the available data do not allow us to determine the timing or pathway of introduction. Human-mediated transport may have contributed to its spread, but the relative importance of each introduction pathway remains unknown” (lines 190-193).Importantly, we added the sentence: “Additional sampling across Haiti and the use of nuclear and/or genomic markers will be necessary to clarify the distribution, population structure and introduction pathways of the species.” (lines 197-199).Also: “and may provide favorable conditions for the establishment” (line 202), and also: “This potential geographic suitability highlights the possibility of further spread into North America, Central and South America and underscores the value for strengthened surveillance and preparedness beyond the Caribbean.” (lines 215-217).And, finally: “Our findings provide the first confirmed record of Aedes vittatus in Haiti and demonstrate its presence in multiple locations. Further surveillance is needed to determine its distribution, extent of establishment,...” (lines 218-220).Inconsistencies in dates and sites / localities should also be corrected.We have carefully checked and corrected inconsistencies in dates and sampling locations to ensure accuracy and coherence across the manuscript (e.g., sampling period until 31 October 2025 but identifications of Ae. vittatus between 7 and 24 of October). Also the number of localities and municipalities listed in Table I).We have revised in the abstract “Larval surveys were done across 18 localities within 12 municipalities in the North and North-East departments of Haiti” (Lines 28-29).In Results: “During the sampling period, Ae. vittatus was detected in 8 of 23 sites (34.7%) across..” (lines 137-138).We added also more molecular identifications of other mosquito species, two species that are reported for the first time in Haiti.In the abstract: “Additional mosquito species were identified, including first records of Cx. garciai and Cx. interrogator in Haiti.”In results: “The COI sequencing confirmed the identification of Ps. pygmaea, Cx. quinquefasciatus, Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus and Cx. interrogator, with the latter showing high similarity to GenBank reference sequences (99.67% identity; MT999299.1). For Culex garciai, no reference sequences are currently available in GenBank; therefore, we generated the first COI sequences for this species in this study.“(lines 178-182).We have also added some clarifications, regarding the molecular work. In material: “...as one of the five samples did not amplify,..” (line107).In the discussion: “Notably, we also reported Cx. garciai and Cx. interrogator from Haiti for the first time. Morphological identification of Cx. interrogator was supported by molecular results, showing high sequence identity but lower query coverage, likely reflecting partial sequences or trimming. (lines 215-218).References are generally relevant and updated, but their formatting should be standardized.We have carefully reviewed and standardized the formatting of all references according to the journal guidelines. The reference list has been thoroughly checked for consistency in authors’ names, journal abbreviations, publication details, page ranges, and DOI formatting. All changes made to the references are indicated in red in the revised manuscript.We believe these revisions have improved the clarity and rigor of the manuscript, and we thank you again for your helpful feedback.Sincerely,David Roiz, in behalf of the authors REVIEWER #1No comments.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to provide evidence of the establishment of Ae. vittatus in Haiti, given its potential role as a vector of chikungunya, dengue, Zika and yellow fever, and its continued expansion across the Caribbean.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Larval surveys were conducted in 18 localities within 12 municipalities in the North and Northeast departments of Haiti, focusing on urban, peri-urban and rural areas during the latter part of the rainy season.
analysis.methods: Mosquito specimens were identified morphologically and confirmed by COI-based DNA barcoding. PCR was performed in duplicate using universal invertebrate-specific primers to amplify a 658-bp fragment of the mitochondrial COI gene, followed by Sanger sequencing and phylogenetic analysis.
analysis.main_results: vittatus was detected in eight of the 23 sites (34.7%) across six municipalities in northern Haiti, with the species found in half of the municipalities sampled.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The detection of Ae. vittatus in one-third of the sampled habitats and half of the surveyed communes, despite limited sampling, indicates that the species is present at multiple localities in northern Haiti.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the need for continued entomological surveillance and early detection in the Caribbean and the Americas, given the potential role of Ae. vittatus as a vector of chikungunya and other arboviruses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The limited sampling effort and the absence of Ae. vittatus in earlier surveys in 2013 suggest the need for further studies to assess its wider distribution and establish the extent of its establishment.

analysis.summary_en: This study reports the first detection of the invasive mosquito species Aedes vittatus in Haiti, confirming its presence in eight of 23 sampled sites across six municipalities in the North department. The species was identified through morphological and molecular methods, including COI-based DNA barcoding and phylogenetic analysis. The findings indicate that Ae. vittatus is present in multiple habitats and communes, despite limited sampling, and highlight its potential role as a vector for chikungunya and other arboviruses. The study underscores the importance of continued entomological surveillance in the Caribbean and the Americas due to the species' ecological plasticity and dispersal capacity. However, the limited sampling effort and absence from earlier surveys suggest the need for further research to fully understand its distribution and establishment. The evidence is moderate, as the study provides direct detection but lacks broader ecological or epidemiological data.

analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The detection of Ae. vittatus in one-third of the sampled habitats and half of the surveyed communes, despite limited sampling, indicates that the species is present at multiple localities in northern Haiti.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the need for continued entomological surveillance and early detection in the Caribbean and the Americas, given the potential role of Ae. vittatus as a vector of chikungunya and other arboviruses.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The limited sampling effort and the absence of Ae. vittatus in earlier surveys in 2013 suggest the need for further studies to assess its wider distribution and establish the extent of its establishment.

title_zh: 海地的威塔斯伊蚊:整个加勒比地区的持续扩张及其对美洲的影响
source_body_en: BACKGROUND Aedes vittatus, an emerging invasive species and arboviral vector with high ecological plasticity and dispersal capacity, is expanding in the Caribbean, being detected in the Dominican Republic, Cuba, and Jamaica and recently in Yucatán, Mexico.OBJECTIVESThis study aimed to provide evidence of the establishment of Ae. MATERIALS AND METHODS Study area - The survey was conducted in the North and Northeast departments of Haiti, restricted to the extensive, low-elevation coastal zones of both regions. The climate varies from tropical monsoon (North Department) to tropical savanna (Northeast Department), with mean annual temperatures of 24 to 28oC and seasonal rainfall (April to November), averaging between 1,000 and 1,500 mm per year, with a decreasing gradient from the coast toward the interior.The study area, located mainly within the coastal plains surrounding the departmental capital, Cap-Haïtien, extends from Limbé (19o42’N, 72o24’W) in the west to Ouanaminthe (19o29’N, 71o46’W), located on the Dominican border, 75 km east of Limbé, following the coastal fringe and reaching up to 20 km inland. (A) Situation map of Haiti within Caribbean countries with presence (green area) and location of capture points (red dots) of Aedes vittatus in neighbouring countries; (B) Delimitation of study area in Haiti (blue rectangle) and location capture (red dots) of Ae. vittatus in Haiti.METHODSLarval surveys were conducted in 18 localities within 12 municipalities in the North and Northeast departments of Haiti. Specimens were identified morphologically and confirmed by COI-based DNA barcoding.FINDINGSWe report, for the first time, the detection of the invasive vector Ae. (Fredwardsius) vittatus in Haiti, confirmed morphologically and molecularly, with the species detected...

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在为Ae的建立提供证据。鉴于其作为基孔肯雅热、登革热、寨卡病毒和黄热病 媒介 的潜在作用,以及其在加勒比地区的持续扩张,海地的 vittatus 已被广泛使用。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 在海地北部和东北部省份 12 个城市的 18 个地点进行了幼虫调查,重点是雨季后期的城市、城郊和农村地区。
analysis_zh.methods: 蚊子标本经过形态学鉴定并通过基于 COI 的 DNA 条形码进行确认。使用通用无脊椎动物特异性引物一式两份地进行 PCR,以扩增线粒体 COI 基因的 658 bp 片段,然后进行桑格测序和系统发育分析。
analysis_zh.main_results: 在海地北部六个城市的 23 个地点中,有 8 个地点(34.7%)检测到了 vittatus,其中一半的采样城市都发现了这种物种。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: Ae的检测。尽管采样有限,但三分之一的采样栖息地和一半的调查社区都发现了 vittatus,这表明该物种存在于海地北部的多个地点。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 鉴于伊蚊的潜在作用,研究结果强调需要在加勒比海和美洲继续进行昆虫学 监测 和早期检测。vittatus 是基孔肯雅热和其他虫媒病毒的 媒介。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 有限的采样工作和缺乏 Ae。2013 年早些时候的调查表明,需要进一步研究来评估其更广泛的分布并确定其建立的程度。

title: Integrated multi-pathogen serosurveillance in children from East New Britain, Papua New Guinea using multiplex bead assays
abstract: Children in Papua New Guinea experience a high burden of infectious diseases, including neglected tropical diseases, arboviral infections, enteric pathogens, and soil-transmitted helminths. Multi-pathogen serological surveillance provides a powerful approach for simultaneously characterising population-level exposure and susceptibility to multiple pathogens, complementing other forms of surveillance and to guide public health decision-making. We collected blood samples from 379 children aged 10 to 24 months (median 16 months) living in East New Britian Papua New Guinea, to assess antibodies to 11 priority pathogens. Seropositivity was highest for Cryptosporidium (52.8%), followed by dengue (30.9%), chikungunya (25.3%), Giardia (13.5%) and malaria parasites (Plasmodium vivax 11.1%; Plasmodium falciparum 5.0%). Males were significantly more likely to be positive for trachoma (10.5% vs 2.2%, p = 0.001). Co-exposure to multiple pathogen groups was common, with approximately 45% of children seropositive for antibodies from two or more different pathogens. While prevalence varied markedly across pathogen groups, these results confirm substantial early-life exposure to multiple endemic pathogens in East New Britain, Papua New Guinea. Simultaneous assessment of multiple pathogens from a single sample demonstrates the value of multiplex serological surveillance and can inform targeted public health interventions.

Multi- 36 pathogen serological surveillance provides a powerful approach for simultaneously characterising 37 population-level exposure and susceptibility to multiple pathogens, complementing other forms of 38 surveillance and to guide public health decision-making. We collected blood samples from 379 children 39 aged 10 to 24 months (median 16 months) living in East New Britian Papua New Guinea, to assess 40 antibodies to 11 priority pathogens. Seropositivity was highest for Cryptosporidium (52.8%), followed 41 by dengue (30.9%), chikungunya (25.3%), Giardia (13.5%) and malaria parasites (Plasmodium vivax 42 11.1%; Plasmodium falciparum 5.0%). Males were significantly more likely to be positive for trachoma 43 (10.5% vs 2.2%, p = 0.001). Co-exposure to multiple pathogen groups was common, with 44 approximately 45% of children seropositive for antibodies from two or more different pathogens. While 45 prevalence varied markedly across pathogen groups, these results confirm substantial early-life 46 exposure to multiple endemic pathogens in East New Britain, Papua New Guinea. Simultaneous 47 assessment of multiple pathogens from a single sample demonstrates the value of multiplex serological 48 surveillance and can inform targeted public health interventions. 49 INTRODUCTION 50 Serological surveillance provides a powerful approach for characterising population-level exposure and 51 susceptibility to infectious diseases, offering insights that complement routine case-based and genomic 52 surveillance [1]. By measuring pathogen-specific antibodies, serosurveys capture cumulative exposure 53 and immune responses that are often missed by conventional surveillance systems, particularly in low- 54 and middle-income settings. In Papua New Guinea (PNG), geographic, logistical, and health system 55 constraints limit the availability and representativeness of routine surveillance data, underscoring the 56 need for scalable approaches that can generate robust epidemiological evidence from existing studies 57 and specimens [2]. 58 Children in PNG experience a high burden of infectious diseases, including neglected tropical diseases, 59 arboviral infections, enteric pathogens, and soil-transmitted helminths, often with repeated or 60 3 concurrent exposures beginning early in life [3-6]. These infections are frequently asymptomatic or 61 underdiagnosed yet can have substantial cumulative impacts on child health. Chronic or recurrent 62 enteric infections and soil transmitted helminths have been associated with impaired linear growth, 63 undernutrition, anaemia, and altered immune function, while repeated arboviral and other endemic 64 infections may further contribute to inflammatory and immunological stress during critical periods of 65 development [7,8]. Understanding patterns of exposure to multiple pathogens in childhood is therefore 66 essential for informing integrated disease control strategies and broader child health interventions. 67 Multiplex bead assay (MBA) technologies enable the simultaneous measurement of antibodies to 68 antigens from multiple pathogens using a single, small-volume specimen. Integrating MBA-based 69 multi-pathogen serosurveillance into demographic health or disease-specific surveys allows efficient 70 assessment of exposure to vaccine preventable diseases, neglected tropical diseases, arboviruses, enteric 71 pathogens, and soil transmitted helminths within the same cohort [9]. This integrated approach supports 72 the identification of co-exposure patterns and overlapping disease burdens that would be difficult to 73 detect using pathogen-specific studies alone. As validated antigen targets continue to expand, MBA 74 platforms also facilitate cross-pathogen analytical approaches that can inform prioritisation of 75 interventions and contribute to efforts to reduce health inequities among children in PNG. 76 This study is a serological sub study nested within a larger study designed to assess population-level 77 immunity to vaccine-preventable diseases in young children in PNG. Leveraging stored samples from 78 the parent study provides a unique opportunity to extend the scientific value of existing data by 79 characterising exposure to a broader range of pathogens without additional sample collection or 80 participant burden [10]. Such an approach is particularly advantageous in paediatric populations, where 81 blood volumes are limited and repeated sampling is ethically and logistically challenging. 82 In this serological sub study, we investigated antibody seroprevalence to 20 antigens from 11 pathogens, 83 including neglected tropical diseases, soil transmitted helminths, malaria, arboviruses, and enteric 84 pathogens, among children aged 10 to 24 months residing in East New Britain Province (ENB), PNG. 85 Children were recruited from five priority local-level government (LLGs) areas encompassing urban, 86 rural, and remote island settings, selected to capture geographic and sociodemographic diversity across 87 4 ENB. This integrated, multi-pathogen approach provides a comprehensive assessment of early-life 88 exposure to endemic infections and generates evidence to inform coordinated child health and disease 89 control strategies in the province. 90 RESULTS 91 Demographic characteristics of the study participants is summarised in Table 1. A total of 379 children 92 aged 10-24 months, with a median age 16 months were enrolled between late March and mid-August 93 2023. Participant numbers were broadly comparable across the five targeted LLG areas, and just over 94 half of the cohort were male (53%). 95 Table 1: Demographic characteristics of participants 96 N (%) Gender Male 200 (53%) Female 179 (47%) Age (months) <12 70 (18%) 12 – <18 169 (45%) 18 – <24 136 (36%) Missing 4 (1%) Local-level government Bitapaka 78 (21%) Duke of York 77 (20%) Inland Baining 66 (17%) Kokopo Urban 81 (21%) Toma-Vunadidir 77 (20%) 97 98 99 100 5 Seroprevalence of pathogens in children 101 Among the 379 children, antibodies to multiple pathogens were detected, with substantial variation in 102 prevalence across the 11 pathogen groups included in the study (Supplementary Figure 1). 103 Seropositivity was highest for Cryptosporidium (Cryptosporidium parvum) (52.8%), followed by 104 dengue virus (30.9%), chikungunya virus (25.3%), Giardia (Giardia lamblia) (13.5%), Plasmodium 105 vivax (11.1%), trachoma (Chlamydia trachomatis) (6.6%), Plasmodium falciparum (5.0%), soil- 106 transmitted helminths (Strongyloides stercoralis or Taenia solium) (2.9%), lymphatic filariasis (1.9%), 107 Zika virus (1.6%) and yaws (Treponema pallidum) (0%). 108 No significant differences in seroprevalence were observed between males and females for most 109 pathogens. However, males were significantly more likely (10.5% vs 2.2%, p = 0.001) to have been 110 exposed to C. Trachomatis (Pgp3). Co-exposure to multiple pathogen groups was common. Of the 11 111 pathogens examined, approximately 25% (N = 93) of children were seropositive for antibodies from 112 two different pathogens, and an additional 20% (N = 77) were seropositive to three or more pathogens, 113 confirming significant exposure to malaria, arboviruses, and neglected tropical diseases in early 114 childhood. 115 116 Figure 1. Heatmap showing overall seroprevalence for the 11 pathogens examined in the study (N = 117 379). 118 6 Does exposure accumulate with age? 119 Serological responses demonstrated substantial heterogeneity in exposure across pathogens and age 120 groups. Antibody responses to Cryptosporidium were consistently high across all age strata, suggesting 121 that exposure occurs early in life. Similarly, seroreactivity to P. vivax was common across the study 122 population, indicating sustained transmission. 123 Clear age-related trends were observed for several pathogens. Seropositivity increased significantly 124 with age for yaws (p = 0.014), dengue virus (p < 0.001), and chikungunya virus (p < 0.001), indicative 125 of increased likelihood of environmental and vector exposure with age. (Figure 2). 126 For several infections, including trachoma (p = 0.035), P. falciparum, Giardia, and soil-transmitted 127 helminths, relatively high seroprevalence was observed among children younger than 12 months and 128 may reflect a combination of maternally derived antibodies and natural exposure. Consistent with this, 129 we observed a rise in seropositivity to P. falciparum, trachoma, Giardia in children aged >18 months, 130 but not 12-18 months, suggesting that antibody responses later in life reflect true exposure and infection 131 acquired during early childhood. 132 Pathogen-specific differences were also evident among the youngest infants. No serological evidence 133 of Zika virus exposure was detected in children younger than 12 months, while detectable antibodies 134 were observed in a small proportion of those children older than 12 months (1.6%). This finding 135 suggests either an absence of recent transmission or very limited exposure within the study population, 136 particularly among younger age groups. 137 138 139 7 140 141 Figure 2. Seroprevalence by age group (N = 379). 142 143 Where is transmission concentrated? 144 Seroprevalence varied across the five local-level government areas despite relatively similar numbers 145 of samples collected from each location, reflecting underlying geographic and sociodemographic 146 heterogeneity across the study sites, which included urban, rural, and remote island settings (Figure 3). 147 These spatial differences suggest heterogeneous patterns of pathogen exposure within the study 148 province. 149 Antibodies to P. vivax malaria were most prevalent in the Duke of York and Toma-Vunadidir LLGs, 150 indicating higher levels of exposure in these areas compared with the other study sites. In contrast, 151 serological evidence of trachoma (based on responses to C. trachomatis antigens) was markedly lower 152 in the Duke of York LLG. Arboviral exposure also showed geographic variation, with antibodies to 153 chikungunya most frequently detected among children living in the Bitapaka and Kokopo Urban LLGs. 154 8 Marked differences were also observed for several other pathogens. Notably, no serological evidence 155 of exposure to P. falciparum malaria or lymphatic filariasis was detected among children sampled from 156 the Inland Baining LLG. In contrast, almost half of children with antibodies to Giardia were from Toma- 157 Vunadidir, suggesting higher levels of transmission of this enteric pathogen in that area. Together, these 158 findings highlight substantial spatial heterogeneity in exposure to malaria, arboviruses, enteric 159 pathogens, and neglected tropical diseases within the study region. 160 161 162 163 164 165 166 167 168 169 170 171 172 173 174 175 176 177 178 179 180 181 9 182 Figure 3. Geographic variation in seroprevalence across five local-level governments (N = 379). 183 184 185 186 187 188 189 190 191 192 193 10 DISCUSSION 194 To our knowledge, this is the first study to apply integrated multi-pathogen serosurveillance in children 195 in PNG, demonstrating the feasibility and added value of this approach for characterising early life 196 exposure to multiple co-endemic pathogens in this setting. Overall, 45% of children had detectable 197 antibodies to multiple pathogens, although pathogen-specific seroprevalence varied by age and 198 geographic location. Seropositivity was highest for Cryptosporidium, followed by the arboviruses 199 dengue and chikungunya, then Giardia, trachoma, and malaria parasites P. vivax malaria and P. 200 falciparum malaria. Seroprevalence for dengue was similar to that of chikungunya, reflecting 201 comparable early-life exposure in this population. The high prevalence of antibodies to enteric 202 pathogens such as Cryptosporidium and Giardia suggests that exposure occurs very early in life, likely 203 reflecting ongoing transmission associated with limited access to clean water, sanitation, and hygiene 204 conditions. While it is widely acknowledged that malaria, particularly Plasmodium vivax, is commonly 205 experienced by children in this age group in PNG [11,12], these findings provide serological evidence that 206 exposure to dengue and chikungunya is similarly prevalent. Data from Pacific Island serosurveys 207 support substantial dengue exposure occurring in early childhood, with seroprevalence among children 208 under five years already approaching 40–50% in some settings [13,14]. This is important for informing 209 both clinical management of febrile illness in young children and the design of targeted public health 210 interventions. 211 Overall, antibodies to enteric pathogens and malaria were most commonly detected, while neglected 212 tropical diseases such as soil-transmitted helminths, trachoma, yaws, and lymphatic filariasis were 213 generally less prevalent. Patterns of seropositivity varied across antigens, suggesting heterogeneous 214 transmission dynamics within the province and highlighting the value of multi-pathogen serological 215 surveillance in this young paediatric population. In 2022, East New Britain Province completed two 216 annual rounds of lymphatic filariasis mass drug administration with the triple drug regimen ivermectin, 217 diethylcarbamazine, and albendazole (IDA) [15]. The limited serological evidence of exposure observed 218 in this study of children surveyed in 2023 is consistent with reduced or interrupted transmission in two 219 LLGs [16]. The presence of detectable antibodies in a subset of children in 3 LLGs suggests that 220 11 transmission likely persists within some areas of ENB [16]. Seroprevalence was generally similar 221 between males and females, suggesting comparable exposure risks during early childhood. The 222 exception was the Pgp3 antigen of C. trachomatis, for which seropositivity was significantly higher in 223 males. This has not been previously observed in other studies of Pgp3 IgG seroprevalence to C. 224 trachomatis in children, which have identified age and community transmission intensity as they key 225 drivers of exposure [17]. Conversely, adult women have been reported to have substantially higher rates 226 of trachomatous scarring and trichiasis than men, widely attributed to gendered exposure over a lifetime 227 [18]. 228 Evidence of exposure to multiple pathogens was common. Approximately one-quarter of children were 229 seropositive for antibodies to two pathogens, and a further one-fifth showed evidence of exposure to 230 three or more pathogens. This pattern highlights the considerable infectious disease burden faced by 231 young children in this setting, where malaria parasites, arboviruses, enteric pathogens, and neglected 232 tropical diseases circulate concurrently. The age-stratified analyses further support this interpretation. 233 Seropositivity increased with age for several pathogens, including dengue, chikungunya, lymphatic 234 filariasis, and yaws, consistent with increasing interaction with people, vectors or environment as 235 children get older. In contrast, seroreactivity to Cryptosporidium remained high across age groups, 236 suggesting that exposure occurs very early in life. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the seroprevalence of multiple pathogens in children in East New Britain, Papua New Guinea, addressing the high burden of infectious diseases in the region.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A multi-pathogen serosurvey was conducted on 379 children aged 10 to 24 months from East New Britain, Papua New Guinea, to evaluate antibodies against 11 priority pathogens.
analysis.methods: Blood samples were collected and analyzed using multiplex bead assays to detect antibodies against the specified pathogens.
analysis.main_results: Seropositivity was highest for Cryptosporidium (52.8%), followed by dengue (30.9%), chikungunya (25.3%), Giardia (13.5%), and malaria parasites (Plasmodium vivax 11.1%; Plasmodium falciparum 5.0%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Males were significantly more likely to be positive for trachoma (10.5% vs 2.2%, p = 0.001), and co-exposure to multiple pathogen groups was common, with approximately 45% of children seropositive for antibodies from two or more different pathogens.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings confirm substantial early-life exposure to multiple endemic pathogens in East New Britain, Papua New Guinea, and highlight the value of multiplex serological surveillance for guiding public health interventions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's design limitations, including the lack of detailed statistical analyses and potential sampling biases, may affect the generalizability of the results.

analysis.summary_en: This study assessed the seroprevalence of multiple pathogens in children from East New Britain, Papua New Guinea, revealing high exposure rates to Cryptosporidium, dengue, and chikungunya, among others. The findings support the use of multiplex serological surveillance for public health decision-making.

elements_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the seroprevalence of multiple pathogens in children in East New Britain, Papua New Guinea, addressing the high burden of infectious diseases in the region.
elements_en.study_design_and_population: A multi-pathogen serosurvey was conducted on 379 children aged 10 to 24 months from East New Britain, Papua New Guinea, to evaluate antibodies against 11 priority pathogens.
elements_en.methods: Blood samples were collected and analyzed using multiplex bead assays to detect antibodies against the specified pathogens.
elements_en.main_results: Seropositivity was highest for Cryptosporidium (52.8%), followed by dengue (30.9%), chikungunya (25.3%), Giardia (13.5%), and malaria parasites (Plasmodium vivax 11.1%; Plasmodium falciparum 5.0%).
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: Males were significantly more likely to be positive for trachoma (10.5% vs 2.2%, p = 0.001), and co-exposure to multiple pathogen groups was common, with approximately 45% of children seropositive for antibodies from two or more different pathogens.
elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings confirm substantial early-life exposure to multiple endemic pathogens in East New Britain, Papua New Guinea, and highlight the value of multiplex serological surveillance for guiding public health interventions.
elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's design limitations, including the lack of detailed statistical analyses and potential sampling biases, may affect the generalizability of the results.
