title_zh: 使用多重微珠检测对东新不列颠、巴布亚新几内亚儿童进行综合多病原体血清监测
source_body_en: Children in Papua New Guinea experience a high burden of infectious diseases, including neglected tropical diseases, arboviral infections, enteric pathogens, and soil-transmitted helminths. Multi-pathogen serological surveillance provides a powerful approach for simultaneously characterising population-level exposure and susceptibility to multiple pathogens, complementing other forms of surveillance and to guide public health decision-making. We collected blood samples from 379 children aged 10 to 24 months (median 16 months) living in East New Britian Papua New Guinea, to assess antibodies to 11 priority pathogens. Seropositivity was highest for Cryptosporidium (52.8%), followed by dengue (30.9%), chikungunya (25.3%), Giardia (13.5%) and malaria parasites (Plasmodium vivax 11.1%; Plasmodium falciparum 5.0%). Males were significantly more likely to be positive for trachoma (10.5% vs 2.2%, p = 0.001). Co-exposure to multiple pathogen groups was common, with approximately 45% of children seropositive for antibodies from two or more different pathogens. While prevalence varied markedly across pathogen groups, these results confirm substantial early-life exposure to multiple endemic pathogens in East New Britain, Papua New Guinea. Simultaneous assessment of multiple pathogens from a single sample demonstrates the value of multiplex serological surveillance and can inform targeted public health interventions.
abstract_zh: 巴布亚新几内亚的儿童承受着沉重的传染病负担,包括被忽视的热带病、虫媒病毒感染、肠道病原体和土源性蠕虫。多病原体血清学 监测 提供了一种强大的方法,可同时表征人​​群水平的暴露和对多种病原体的易感性,补充其他形式的 监测 并指导公共卫生决策。我们收集了居住在东新不列颠巴布亚新几内亚的 379 名 10 至 24 个月(中位 16 个月)儿童的血液样本,以评估针对 11 种重点病原体的抗体。隐孢子虫的血清阳性率最高(52.8%),其次是登革热(30.9%)、基孔肯雅热(25.3%)、贾第鞭毛虫(13.5%)和疟疾寄生虫(间日疟原虫11.1%;恶性疟原虫5.0%)。男性沙眼阳性的可能性明显更高(10.5% vs 2.2%,p = 0.001)。同时接触多种病原体组很常见,大约 45% 的儿童对来自两种或多种不同病原体的抗体呈血清反应阳性。虽然 患病率 在不同病原体群体之间存在显着差异,但这些结果证实了巴布亚新几内亚东新不列颠地区在生命早期大量接触多种地方性病原体。对单个样本中多种病原体的同时评估证明了多重血清学 监测 的价值,并且可以为有针对性的公共卫生干预措施提供信息。

title: Presence of Heterozygous V1016G kdr Mutation in Pyrethroid Insecticide Resistance in Aedes aegypti a Dengue vector from Southern India

full_text: Abstract Background Aedes aegypti is a primary vector of Dengue, Chikungunya, and Zika viruses, and its control relies heavily on pyrethroid insecticides. However, the development of resistance in mosquito populations poses a major challenge to effective vector control. This study aimed to investigate the presence of the V1016G knockdown resistance (kdr) mutation in Aedes aegypti collected from Nagapattinam district, Tamil Nadu, India. Methods Aedes immatures were collected from selected field sites and subjected to insecticide susceptibility testing using World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines. Genomic DNA was extracted, and allele-specific PCR was performed to detect the V1016G mutation in the voltage-gated sodium channel gene (vgsc). Results The analysis revealed the presence of the V1016G mutation in heterozygous form (VG) among the tested samples. No homozygous mutants (GG) were detected. The presence of heterozygous individuals indicates an early stage of resistance development, likely due to ongoing insecticide selection pressure. Bioassay results showed reduced susceptibility to pyrethroids in these populations, supporting the molecular findings. Conclusion This study provides baseline data on the genetic mechanism of pyrethroid resistance in Aedes aegypti from Nagapattinam district. Regular monitoring of kdr mutations is essential to detect resistance early and guide insecticide use policies. Integrating molecular surveillance with conventional control measures will help delay the spread of resistance and improve the long-term success of vector management programs. The findings highlight the need for alternative control strategies and responsible insecticide use to maintain the effectiveness of current interventions. full_text_sections.full_text: Abstract Background Aedes aegypti is a primary vector of Dengue, Chikungunya, and Zika viruses, and its control relies heavily on pyrethroid insecticides. However, the development of resistance in mosquito populations poses a major challenge to effective vector control. This study aimed to investigate the presence of the V1016G knockdown resistance (kdr) mutation in Aedes aegypti collected from Nagapattinam district, Tamil Nadu, India. Methods Aedes immatures were collected from selected field sites and subjected to insecticide susceptibility testing using World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines. Genomic DNA was extracted, and allele-specific PCR was performed to detect the V1016G mutation in the voltage-gated sodium channel gene (vgsc). Results The analysis revealed the presence of the V1016G mutation in heterozygous form (VG) among the tested samples. No homozygous mutants (GG) were detected. The presence of heterozygous individuals indicates an early stage of resistance development, likely due to ongoing insecticide selection pressure. Bioassay results showed reduced susceptibility to pyrethroids in these populations, supporting the molecular findings. Conclusion This study provides baseline data on the genetic mechanism of pyrethroid resistance in Aedes aegypti from Nagapattinam district. Regular monitoring of kdr mutations is essential to detect resistance early and guide insecticide use policies. Integrating molecular surveillance with conventional control measures will help delay the spread of resistance and improve the long-term success of vector management programs. The findings highlight the need for alternative control strategies and responsible insecticide use to maintain the effectiveness of current interventions. analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the presence of the V1016G kdr mutation in Aedes aegypti from Nagapattinam district, Tamil Nadu, India, as a potential indicator of pyrethroid resistance. The research aimed to understand the genetic basis of resistance in this mosquito population, which is a primary vector for Dengue, Chikungunya, and Zika viruses. Methods included genomic DNA extraction and allele-specific PCR to detect the mutation, alongside insecticide susceptibility testing using WHO guidelines. Results showed the V1016G mutation in heterozygous form but no homozygous mutants, with bioassays confirming reduced susceptibility to pyrethroids. The authors interpreted these findings as an early stage of resistance development due to insecticide selection pressure. The study provides baseline data for molecular surveillance of resistance in Aedes aegypti, highlighting the need for integrated control strategies. However, the study's limitations include a lack of generalisability and detailed statistical analysis, resulting in moderate confidence in the evidence.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在调查从印度泰米尔纳德邦 Nagapattinam 区采集的埃及伊蚊中是否存在 V1016G 击倒抗性 (kdr) 突变。埃及伊蚊是登革热、基孔肯雅热和寨卡病毒的主要 媒介,其控制严重依赖拟除虫菊酯类杀虫剂。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及从选定的田间地点收集未成熟的伊蚊,并根据世界卫生组织(WHO)的指导方针对它们进行杀虫剂敏感性测试。提取基因组DNA,进行等位基因特异性PCR检测电压门控钠通道基因(vgsc)中的V1016G 突变。
elements_zh.methods: 从埃及伊蚊样本中提取基因组DNA,进行等位基因特异性PCR检测电压门控钠通道基因中的V1016G 突变。根据世界卫生组织指南进行杀虫剂敏感性测试,以评估耐药性水平。
elements_zh.main_results: 分析显示,测试样本中存在杂合形式 (VG) 的 V1016G 突变。没有检测到纯合突变体(GG)。生物测定结果显示这些人群对拟除虫菊酯的敏感性降低,支持了分子发现。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 杂合个体的存在表明抗性发展的早期阶段,可能是由于持续的杀虫剂选择压力。本研究提供了 Nagapattinam 地区埃及伊蚊拟除虫菊酯抗性遗传机制的基线数据。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 定期监测 kdr 突变 对于及早发现抗性并指导杀虫剂使用政策至关重要。将分子 监测 与常规控制措施相结合将有助于延缓耐药性的传播并提高 媒介 管理计划的长期成功率。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究没有报告研究结果的普遍性或证据的强度,但分子和生物测定结果是一致的并支持解释。由于研究范围有限,证据不充分。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在调查从印度泰米尔纳德邦 Nagapattinam 区采集的埃及伊蚊中是否存在 V1016G 击倒抗性 (kdr) 突变。埃及伊蚊是登革热、基孔肯雅热和寨卡病毒的主要 媒介,其控制严重依赖拟除虫菊酯类杀虫剂。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及从选定的田间地点收集未成熟的伊蚊,并根据世界卫生组织(WHO)的指导方针对它们进行杀虫剂敏感性测试。提取基因组DNA,进行等位基因特异性PCR检测电压门控钠通道基因(vgsc)中的V1016G 突变。
analysis_zh.methods: 从埃及伊蚊样本中提取基因组DNA,进行等位基因特异性PCR检测电压门控钠通道基因中的V1016G 突变。根据世界卫生组织指南进行杀虫剂敏感性测试,以评估耐药性水平。
analysis_zh.main_results: 分析显示,测试样本中存在杂合形式 (VG) 的 V1016G 突变。没有检测到纯合突变体(GG)。生物测定结果显示这些人群对拟除虫菊酯的敏感性降低,支持了分子发现。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 杂合个体的存在表明抗性发展的早期阶段,可能是由于持续的杀虫剂选择压力。本研究提供了 Nagapattinam 地区埃及伊蚊拟除虫菊酯抗性遗传机制的基线数据。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 定期监测 kdr 突变 对于及早发现抗性并指导杀虫剂使用政策至关重要。将分子 监测 与常规控制措施相结合将有助于延缓耐药性的传播并提高 媒介 管理计划的长期成功率。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究没有报告研究结果的普遍性或证据的强度,但分子和生物测定结果是一致的并支持解释。由于研究范围有限,证据不充分。

title: Rainfall and human activities drive Aedes aegypti breeding sites infestation and larval density in urban and rural settings of Bobo-Dioulasso in western Burkina Faso
abstract: Aedes aegypti , the primary vector of dengue, chikungunya and Zika, breeds mainly in artificial containers around households, and its larval abundance reflects a complex interplay between climate and human practices. In our cross-sectional survey conducted in urban and rural sectors of Bobo-Dioulasso across dry and rainy seasons, entomological indices exceeded WHO epidemic thresholds, with the House Index reaching 66.7% and the Breteau Index ranging from 107 to 147, indicating sustained transmission risk. Infestation varied markedly by container type. Domestic materials (41.9%), basins (29.4%) and flower pots (28.6%) showed the highest positivity rates, whereas kettles and animal skins were rarely colonized. Notably, although less frequent, terracotta jars, barrels, tires and miscellaneous containers produced more than 70% of all larvae, identifying them as principal production sites. This confirms that structural characteristics of containers, rather than their abundance alone, decisively shape larval habitat suitability. Seasonality also structured larval dynamics. More containers were positive during the dry season, but mean density was three-fold higher in the rainy season, with rainfall exhibiting a non-linear relationship, intermediate precipitation promoting proliferation. After accounting for climatic variables, urban households consistently harbored higher larval densities, reflecting intensive water storage and inadequate waste management. Collectively, proliferation is driven by the combined effects of rainfall dynamics and human practices. Container-related structural and ecological factors, type, exposure and organic matter, therefore exert a more pronounced influence on larval productivity than mere container availability. Interventions should prioritize highly productive containers, particularly jars, barrels and tires, by integrating rainfall-based surveillance with community-led source reduction in areas at greatest transmission risk.

Notably, although less frequent, terracotta jars, barrels, tires and miscellaneous containers produced more than 70% of all larvae, identifying them as principal production sites. This confirms that structural characteristics of containers, rather than their abundance alone, decisively shape larval habitat suitability. Seasonality also structured larval dynamics. More containers were positive during the dry season, but mean density was three-fold higher in the rainy season, with rainfall exhibiting a non-linear relationship, intermediate precipitation promoting proliferation. Introduction Arthropod-borne viruses (arboviruses), particularly those transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, constitute an increasing public health concern in sub-Saharan Africa. Among these diseases, dengue is the most prevalent and poses the greatest public health burden, with more than half of the global population at risk and an estimated 100–400 million infections occurring annually [1]. In Burkina Faso, the epidemiology of dengue has changed markedly over the past decade, with successive outbreaks reported in 2016, 2017, and, most notably, in 2023, when the country experienced its largest documented epidemic [2–4]. Recent entomological investigations have identified Aedes aegypti as the principal vector responsible for dengue transmission in the country [5, 6] . Aedes aegypti is a highly anthropophilic mosquito that has successfully adapted to human-modified environments, enabling its persistence and expansion in rapidly urbanizing areas[7]. The abundance and distribution of this mosquito are governed by the interaction between climatic conditions and anthropogenic environmental changes. Rainfall directly influences the availability of breeding habitats by creating both natural and artificial water-holding containers, thereby promoting immature mosquito development [8, 9]. However, anthropogenic activities substantially amplify these effects by increasing the number and diversity of artificial larval habitats. Discarded tires, water storage jars and barrels, plastic containers, metal cans, construction debris and abandoned vehicles provide highly productive breeding sites that can sustain Ae. aegypti populations even during prolonged dry periods, when natural aquatic habitats become scarce [7, 10, 11]. In addition, household practices such as domestic water storage, inadequate solid waste management and poor environmental sanitation further enhance larval habitat availability and contribute to persistent vector proliferation. Page 3/19 Bobo-Dioulasso, the second largest city in Burkina Faso provides an ideal setting for investigating the interactions between climatic and anthropogenic drivers of Ae. aegypti abundance. Located within the Sudanian climatic zone, the city comprises densely populated urban neighborhoods surrounded by peri-urban and rural communities, creating a pronounced gradient of environmental conditions human activities, and infrastructure [12, 13]. Urban neighborhoods are characterized by high human population density, irregular water supply, widespread domestic water storage and inadequate solid waste management, all of which generate abundant and persistent breeding habitats for Ae. Aegypti [6, 12, 14, 15]. Conversely, rural areas are more strongly influenced by seasonal rainfall which creates transient breeding sites such as tree holes and temporary pools while household water storage practices allow vector populations to persist throughout the dry season [16]. Although rainfall and anthropogenic factors are widely recognized as key determinants of Ae. aegypti ecology, their combined influence on mosquito abundance has received limited attention in Burkina Faso, particularly across urban-rural gradients. Most previous studies have focused either on seasonal variation of vector populations or upon characterization of breeding habitats without explicitly quantifying the interactive effects of climatic and human-related factors on larval density. Addressing this knowledge gap is essential for developing integrated and context-specific vector control strategies that incorporate both environmental variability and human behavioral determinants [17]. In this study, we investigated the combined effects of rainfall and anthropogenic activities on Aedes aegypti density across urban and rural settings in Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. Specifically, we quantified larval density and standard entomological indices during the dry and rainy seasons and assessed the influence of climatic variables and container characteristics on larval abundance. Our findings provide evidence to support targeted, context-specific vector control interventions in areas at high risk of arboviral transmission. Materials and Methods Study area The study was conducted in Bobo-Dioulasso (11°11′N, 4°17′W), the second largest city in Burkina Faso, located at Guiriko Region in the southwestern part of the country (Figure 1). The city lies within the Sudanian climatic zone, which is characterized by two distinct seasons: a rainy season extending from May to October and a dry season from November to April. Annual rainfall ranges between 900 and 1,200 mm, while mean annual temperatures vary from 25°C to 32°C. This climatic regime provides favorable conditions for the seasonal development of Aedes aegypti populations. Two study sites with contrasting ecological and socio-environmental characteristics were selected to represent urban and rural settings within the city: Sector 6 (urban) and Sector 33 (rural) (Figure 1). Selection and description of study sites Urban site (Sector 6) Sector 6 was selected to represent the urban setting because of its position, planned residential layout, and relatively well- developed urban infrastructure. According to the RGPH 2019, sector 6 has a population of 12,266 and comprises 2,926 households. The area is characterized by paved roads, a formal drainage network for wastewater and stormwater, and access to piped water, electricity, health facilities, schools and municipal waste collection services. Housing is predominantly constructed with cement blocks and arranged in planned residential plots. Despite these urban amenities, numerous artificial water-holding containers capable of supporting Ae. aegypti breeding were observed around households including discarded tires, plastic containers, flower pots, blocked drains and domestic water-storage containers. These breeding habitats are largely associated with human activities and urban waste accumulation. Page 4/19 Rural site (Sector 33) Although administratively part of the city of Bobo‐Dioulasso, sector 33 displays ecological and socio‐economic characteristics typical of rural settings (limited infrastructure, reliance on water storage, and proximity to vegetated areas). For this reason, we refer to it as a rural site in the present study. According to the RGPH 2019, sector 33 has a population of 27,251 and comprises 5,956 households. Most houses are constructed from traditional materials (banco or adobe) and potential mosquito breeding habitats consisted of both natural and artificial water-holding sites, including three holes, leaf axils temporary rain-filled puddles, watering troughs, buckets and domestic water-storage containers. Compared with the urban site, aquatic habitats were generally more dispersed and frequently associated with agricultural and household activities. Rationale for site selection The two study sites were selected to capture the environmental and anthropogenic heterogeneity that characterizes Bobo-Dioulasso. Sector 6 represents a highly urbanized environment where vector breeding is primarily associated with artificial containers generated by human activities, intensive urbanization, and high population density. Conversely, Sector 33 represents a predominantly rural environment, where mosquito breeding habitats arise from a combination of natural water collections and domestic water-storage practices under conditions of limited infrastructure. Comparing these contrasting settings provides an opportunity to evaluate how rainfall, sanitation infrastructure, waste management, housing characteristics and water-storage practices influence Aedes aegypti larval abundance under different ecological and socio-economic conditions within the same metropolitan area (Figure 2). This urban-rural comparison also enables the identification of context-specific determinants of vector proliferation that may inform targeted surveillance and control strategies. Study design and data collection Prior to conducting the larval surveys, verbal informed consent was obtained from the head of each household. This study was conducted in two contrasting sites within Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso: Sector 6 (urban) and Sector 33 (rural). Entomological surveys were carried out during the dry season (February, April, and December 2025) and the rainy season (June, September, and October 2025). Thirty (30) households per site were visited during each survey campaign. During each survey, every water-holding container found within each visited concession was systematically inspected. All inspected containers were recorded using a tablet equipped with a standardized data collection form specifically designed for this study. For each container, the following data were recorded: sector, concession identifier, container type, presence or absence of water, presence or absence of larvae (including larval stage) or pupae, water source (rainwater, borehole water, or National Office for Water and Sanitation (ONEA) tap water), water clarity (clear, turbid, or purulent), and presence of vegetation around and inside the container. When larvae or pupae were present, they were collected using a pipette or dipper, transferred into a labelled container and transported to the laboratory. Upon arrival at the laboratory, each container was opened by number, emptied and treated to remove impurities. Larval identification was performed using standard morphological keys based on the respiratory siphon: Anopheles larvae lack a siphon, Aedes larvae possess a short siphon and Culex larvae possess a long siphon [18]. After identification, larvae were counted and the count was recorded directly into the tablet. These data were subsequently used to calculate larval density, entomological indices (Breteau Index, House Index, Container Index) [19] and the density of positive breeding sites per concession. Page 5/19 Data management and statistical analysis All field data were collected using standardized entomological survey forms and entered into a secure database (Microsoft Excel 2016). Three classical entomological indices were calculated to assess the level of Aedes aegypti infestation across sites and seasons: Breteau Index (BI): number of positive containers per 100 inspected premises. House Index (HI): percentage of premises positive for at least one container with Aedes larvae. Container Index (CI): percentage of water‐holding containers positive for Aedes larvae. All statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.3.2) [20], with the significance threshold set at α = 0.05. To evaluate the impact of rainfall and anthropogenic activities on larval density, a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with a negative binomial distribution was fitted. Larval count was used as the response variable, while site (urban vs. rural), season, rainfall, temperature and humidity were included as fixed effects. Concession ID and collection date were treated as random effects to account for repeated measures. Pearson correlation analysis was conducted to explore relationships among environmental parameters and their association with larval abundance. Differences in mean larval densities across sites and seasons were tested using ANOVA, followed by Tukey’s post hoc comparisons when significant differences were detected. Results General description of sampling A total of 816 water-holding containers were inspected across the study area. The most frequently encountered container types were kettles (19.1%, 95% CI: 16.4-21.8), terracotta jars (18.4%, 95% CI: 15.8-21.1) and barrels (16.1%, 95% CI: 13.6- 18.6). Tires (12.0%, 95% CI: 9.8-14.3) and cans (10.7%, 95% CI: 8.6-12.9) also represented a substantial proportion of inspected containers, while watering holes (8.6%), buckets (4.3%), domestic materials (3.8%), flower pots (2.6%), basins (2.1%) and animal skins (0.2%) were less common. Positivity rates varied across container types: terracotta jars (18.0%), barrels (13.0%), tires (21.4%), cans (27.6%), watering holes (21.4%), buckets (22.9%), domestic materials (41.9%), flower pots (28.6%) and basins (29.4%) showed notable proportions of positive containers whereas kettles (5.8%) and animal skins (0%) had the lowest positivity. Page 2/19 Abstract Aedes aegypti, the primary vector of dengue, chikungunya and Zika, breeds mainly in artificial containers around households, and its larval abundance reflects a complex interplay between climate and human practices. In our cross- sectional survey conducted in urban and rural sectors of Bobo-Dioulasso across dry and rainy seasons, entomological indices exceeded WHO epidemic thresholds, with the House Index reaching 66.7% and the Breteau Index ranging from 107 to 147, indicating sustained transmission risk. Infestation varied markedly by container type. Domestic materials (41.9%), basins (29.4%) and flower pots (28.6%) showed the highest positivity rates, whereas kettles and animal skins were rarely colonized. Notably, although less frequent, terracotta jars, barrels, tires and miscellaneous containers produced more than 70% of all larvae, identifying them as principal production sites. This confirms that structural characteristics of containers, rather than their abundance alone, decisively shape larval habitat suitability. Seasonality also structured larval dynamics. More containers were positive during the dry season, but mean density was three-fold higher in the rainy season, with rainfall exhibiting a non-linear relationship, intermediate precipitation promoting proliferation. After accounting for climatic variables, urban households consistently harbored higher larval densities, reflecting intensive water storage and inadequate waste management. Collectively, proliferation is driven by the combined effects of rainfall dynamics and human practices. Container-related structural and ecological factors, type, exposure and organic matter, therefore exert a more pronounced influence on larval productivity than mere container availability. Interventions should prioritize highly productive containers, particularly jars, barrels and tires, by integrating rainfall-based surveillance with community-led source reduction in areas at greatest transmission risk. Introduction Arthropod-borne viruses (arboviruses), particularly those transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, constitute an increasing public health concern in sub-Saharan Africa. Among these diseases, dengue is the most prevalent and poses the greatest public health burden, with more than half of the global population at risk and an estimated 100–400 million infections occurring annually [1]. In Burkina Faso, the epidemiology of dengue has changed markedly over the past decade, with successive outbreaks reported in 2016, 2017, and, most notably, in 2023, when the country experienced its largest documented epidemic [2–4]. Recent entomological investigations have identified Aedes aegypti as the principal vector responsible for dengue transmission in the country [5, 6] . Aedes aegypti is a highly anthropophilic mosquito that has successfully adapted to human-modified environments, enabling its persistence and expansion in rapidly urbanizing areas[7]. The abundance and distribution of this mosquito are governed by the interaction between climatic conditions and anthropogenic environmental changes. Rainfall directly influences the availability of breeding habitats by creating both natural and artificial water-holding containers, thereby promoting immature mosquito development [8, 9]. However, anthropogenic activities substantially amplify these effects by increasing the number and diversity of artificial larval habitats. Discarded tires, water storage jars and barrels, plastic containers, metal cans, construction debris and abandoned vehicles provide highly productive breeding sites that can sustain Ae. aegypti populations even during prolonged dry periods, when natural aquatic habitats become scarce [7, 10, 11]. In addition, household practices such as domestic water storage, inadequate solid waste management and poor environmental sanitation further enhance larval habitat availability and contribute to persistent vector proliferation. Page 3/19 Bobo-Dioulasso, the second largest city in Burkina Faso provides an ideal setting for investigating the interactions between climatic and anthropogenic drivers of Ae. aegypti abundance. Located within the Sudanian climatic zone, the city comprises densely populated urban neighborhoods surrounded by peri-urban and rural communities, creating a pronounced gradient of environmental conditions human activities, and infrastructure [12, 13]. Urban neighborhoods are characterized by high human population density, irregular water supply, widespread domestic water storage and inadequate solid waste management, all of which generate abundant and persistent breeding habitats for Ae. Aegypti [6, 12, 14, 15]. Conversely, rural areas are more strongly influenced by seasonal rainfall which creates transient breeding sites such as tree holes and temporary pools while household water storage practices allow vector populations to persist throughout the dry season [16]. Although rainfall and anthropogenic factors are widely recognized as key determinants of Ae. aegypti ecology, their combined influence on mosquito abundance has received limited attention in Burkina Faso, particularly across urban-rural gradients. Most previous studies have focused either on seasonal variation of vector populations or upon characterization of breeding habitats without explicitly quantifying the interactive effects of climatic and human-related factors on larval density. Addressing this knowledge gap is essential for developing integrated and context-specific vector control strategies that incorporate both environmental variability and human behavioral determinants [17]. In this study, we investigated the combined effects of rainfall and anthropogenic activities on Aedes aegypti density across urban and rural settings in Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. Specifically, we quantified larval density and standard entomological indices during the dry and rainy seasons and assessed the influence of climatic variables and container characteristics on larval abundance. Our findings provide evidence to support targeted, context-specific vector control interventions in areas at high risk of arboviral transmission. abstract_zh: 埃及伊蚊 是登革热、基孔肯雅热和寨卡病毒的主要 媒介,主要在家庭周围的人造容器中繁殖,其幼虫丰度反映了气候与人类活动之间复杂的相互作用。我们在旱季和雨季对博博迪乌拉索城乡进行的横断面调查显示,昆虫学指数超过了世界卫生组织的流行阈值,House指数达到66.7%,Breteau指数在107至147之间,表明传播风险持续存在。感染情况因容器类型而异。国内材料(41.9%)、盆(29.4%)和花盆(28.6%)的阳性率最高,而水壶和兽皮很少被定植。值得注意的是,虽然频率较低,但赤陶罐、桶、轮胎和杂项容器产生了 70% 以上的幼虫,将它们确定为主要生产地。这证实了容器的结构特征,而不是其数量本身,决定了幼虫栖息地的适宜性。季节性也影响了幼虫的动态。旱季更多的集装箱呈阳性,但雨季平均密度高出三倍,降雨量呈现非线性关系,中间降水促进扩散。考虑到气候变量后,城市家庭的幼虫密度始终较高,反映出密集的蓄水和废物管理不足。总的来说,扩散是由降雨动态和人类活动的综合影响驱动的。因此,与容器相关的结构和生态因素、类型、暴露和有机物对幼虫生产力的影响比单纯容器可用性的影响更为显着。干预措施应优先考虑高生产力的容器,特别是罐子、桶和轮胎,将基于降雨的 传播 与社区主导的 传播 风险最大地区的源头减少相结合。
